criterion_notes.c1: Examines household and room-cluster drinking-water supply access (alongside public space access) in an informal settlement (bosti) in Dhaka, covering formal DWASA network exclusion, informal piped water vending, deep-water tube-wells, and vending points.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading of Criterion 2. Plain reading: examines urban water governance, statutory institutions (DWASA), political patronage, and informal committees. Narrow rule-type reading: directly examines (1) statutory land-tenure eligibility rules barring settlements on public land from direct DWASA water connections, (2) regulatory reform under DWASA Rules 2007 mandating water supply to slum committees regardless of land tenure and partial legalisation of vendor connections, (3) selective enforcement and official discretion/accommodation by DWASA inspectors and staff (unofficial payments and temporary line disconnection during inspections), and (4) landlord (room-owner) tenure/contractual gatekeeping over tenant water connections and NGO facility management committees.
criterion_notes.c3: Qualitative socio-legal and ethnographic empirical case study conducted between 2008 and 2010 using Venn diagrams, solicited photography, narrative and in-depth interviews, theoretical sampling, and participant observation (including overnight stays), supplemented by settlement-level descriptive figures on vendor coverage, consumption, continuity, and pricing.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports concrete water access outcomes including exclusion from direct formal DWASA service and stalled 2010 network delivery, household/room-cluster connection coverage (~85% connected via informal piped vendors vs. excluded tenants relying on vending points, wells, and lake water), water quantity (8–44 litres per capita per day), continuity (supply disruptions 3–6 days per month), and affordability (unit water prices 4 to 13 times higher than regular DWASA tariffs).
criterion_notes.c5: Population and units of analysis (households/tenants, room-cluster owners, 50 water vendors, and local committees across ~7,700 households in one Dhaka bosti), rule-type exposures, water access/quantity/continuity/affordability outcomes, and qualitative empirical case-study design are all clearly identifiable.

evidence_quotes.quote: Due to the fact that this bosti has developed through encroaching on government land and is therefore “illegal” to the state, its inhabitants cannot access water directly from the public water supply authority, the Dhaka Water Supply and Sewerage Authority (DWASA).

It is due to about a decade of advocacy by a local NGO and the success of some NGO-run pilot water supply projects in selected bosti of Dhaka that DWASA has been given the mandate to supply water to “slum” committees regardless of land tenure considerations (GOB, 2007).

The paper is based on empirical research conducted between 2008 and 2010. For investigation of both the negotiation of access to public space and the negotiation of water supply a qualitative research methodology was applied.

In the area studied, 50 vendors supply water to about 7,700 households and to businesses needing water (e.g. restaurants, vegetable shops). About 85% of total households have direct water connections to their room clusters, while the households living in the rest of the room clusters collect drinking water from nearby water reservoirs and vending locations.
Per capita daily water consumption in this bosti is therefore only between 8 litres and 44 litres, which is further reduced by regular disruptions in supply on three to six days a month.
Accordingly, the unit price of water in the room clusters of this bosti is about four to thirteen times higher than what the DWASA charges for a regular supply to non-bosti inhabitants.

raw_response.exposure: Statutory land-tenure requirements barring informal settlements on public land from direct DWASA piped water connections; DWASA Rules 2007 permitting water supply through slum committees regardless of tenure; selective enforcement and informal accommodation by DWASA inspectors/officials; and room-owner contractual gatekeeping over informal vendor lines and NGO water committees.
raw_response.outcome: Direct formal utility exclusion, informal room-cluster piped water connection vs. tenant reliance on vending points and wells (~85% room-cluster connection coverage), per capita water quantity (8–44 L/day), supply continuity (disruptions 3–6 days/month), and affordability/tariff burden (unit prices 4–13 times the regular DWASA tariff).
raw_response.population_and_sample: Inhabitants (tenants and room-cluster owners), 50 informal water vendors, local political/social/mosque committees, and institutional informants in a low-income informal settlement (bosti) on public land in Dhaka, Bangladesh (~7,700 households), sampled theoretically during 2008–2010 fieldwork.
raw_response.rationale: This qualitative socio-legal empirical study (2008–2010) examines household drinking-water access in an informal settlement (bosti) of Dhaka, Bangladesh. It meets all inclusion criteria, including the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2, because it empirically analyses how statutory tenure rules excluding settlements on public land from direct DWASA connections, the 2007 DWASA rule change permitting supply via slum committees regardless of tenure, selective DWASA inspection enforcement/bribery, and landlord-tenant contractual mediation shape household water connections, quantity, continuity, exclusion, and affordability. Qualitative empirical studies are eligible for systematic-review mechanism synthesis even without a quantitative effect size.
raw_response.study_design: Qualitative ethnographic and participatory empirical case study (2008–2010) using Venn diagrams, solicited photography, narrative and in-depth interviews, theoretical sampling, and participant observation.
